2018-Q21.shortcut: Weight has a true zero and meaningful ratios, so it is RATIO scale, not interval - statement 1 fails. Statements 2 and 3 are textbook-correct, so the answer is 2 and 3 only.
tips: Scale ladder: nominal (labels) < ordinal (ranks) < interval (equal gaps, arbitrary zero) < ratio (true zero). Weight, length, income and counts are ratio; temperature in Celsius and calendar dates are interval.
The single discriminator for interval vs ratio is 'is zero meaningful?'. Zero weight means no weight, so weight is ratio.
Cross-sectional = many units at ONE time point; time series = one unit over MANY time points; panel = both. 'Each IIM in 2007' is many units, one year, so cross-sectional.
Barcodes, PIN codes, jersey numbers and Aadhaar numbers are all nominal even though they look numeric - arithmetic on them is meaningless.
solution: Statement 1: the weight of a strawberry box is a physical measurement with an absolute zero point, and ratios such as 'twice as heavy' are meaningful. That is the definition of a RATIO scale, not an interval scale. FALSE.
Statement 2: the number of students admitted to each IIM in 2007 records many different units (the IIMs) at a single point in time. That is cross-sectional data. TRUE.
Statement 3: a barcode is only an identifying label; the numbers cannot be ordered or added meaningfully, so the measurement is on a nominal scale. TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct, so option (c) is right.

2018-Q22.shortcut: Var(Y - aX) is a quadratic in a; minimising it is exactly least squares. The minimum is the residual variance of the regression of Y on X, which is Var(Y)(1 - rho^2).
tips: Remember the identity: minimum residual variance = (1 - rho^2) x Var(Y). The factor (1 - rho^2) is the proportion of variance NOT explained; rho^2 is the proportion explained.
Dimensional check kills two options instantly: the answer must have the units of Var(Y). Options (a) and (b) are ratios of variances and are dimensionally wrong.
The minimising value is a = Cov(X,Y)/Var(X), which is precisely the regression coefficient b_(YX) - the question is least squares in disguise.
If rho = 0 the minimum must equal Var(Y) (X is useless); if rho = +-1 it must be 0. Only option (d) satisfies both limits.
solution: Write g(a) = Var(Y - aX) = Var(Y) - 2a Cov(X,Y) + a^2 Var(X). This is an upward parabola in a.
Setting g'(a) = -2 Cov(X,Y) + 2a Var(X) = 0 gives the minimising value a* = Cov(X,Y)/Var(X).
Substituting back: g(a*) = Var(Y) - [Cov(X,Y)]^2/Var(X).
Since rho = Cov(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y)), we have [Cov(X,Y)]^2 = rho^2 Var(X) Var(Y), so [Cov(X,Y)]^2/Var(X) = rho^2 Var(Y).
Therefore the minimum value is Var(Y) - rho^2 Var(Y) = (1 - rho^2) Var(Y).
Hence option (d) is correct.

2018-Q23.shortcut: Use the empirical (median) form of Pearson's skewness: Sk = 3(Mean - Median)/SD. So -0.3 = 3(62 - 65)/SD = -9/SD, giving SD = 30.
tips: Two forms of Pearson's coefficient: (Mean - Mode)/SD and 3(Mean - Median)/SD. When the MEDIAN is supplied, the factor 3 is compulsory - dropping it gives SD = 10, which is planted as option (a).
The sign works out automatically: mean below median gives a negative numerator and hence negative skewness, consistent with the given -0.3.
The relation comes from the empirical mode formula Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, which is worth memorising in its own right.
Sanity check the magnitude: |Mean - Median| = 3 and the coefficient is small (0.3), so the SD must be an order of magnitude larger than 3 - that alone points to 30.
solution: Pearson's coefficient of skewness in its median form is Sk = 3(Mean - Median)/SD.
Substitute the given values: -0.3 = 3(62 - 65)/SD.
The numerator is 3 x (-3) = -9, so -0.3 = -9/SD.
Hence the standard deviation is 30, option (b).

tips: Yule's coefficient of association Q = (ad - bc)/(ad + bc) always lies between -1 and +1; it is 0 exactly when ad = bc, i.e. under independence.

Set the 2x2 table out as a = both present, b and c = one present, d = both absent. Here the diagonal product ad = 1500 dominates the off-diagonal bc = 100, so the association must be strongly POSITIVE - that alone eliminates (c).
Do not confuse Yule's Q with the coefficient of colligation Y = (sqrt(ad) - sqrt(bc))/(sqrt(ad) + sqrt(bc)), which would give a different value here.
Sons of smokers smoking 50:10 while sons of non-smokers smoke 10:30 is a clear positive association - a quick common-sense check on the sign before computing.
solution: Arrange the 2x2 contingency table: (AB) = 50 (both smoke), (A beta) = 10 (father smokes, son does not), (alpha B) = 10 (father does not, son does), (alpha beta) = 30 (neither smokes).
Yule's coefficient of association is Q = [(AB)(alpha beta) - (A beta)(alpha B)] / [(AB)(alpha beta) + (A beta)(alpha B)].
Diagonal product: (AB)(alpha beta) = 50 x 30 = 1500.
Off-diagonal product: (A beta)(alpha B) = 10 x 10 = 100.
The value is positive and close to 1, indicating strong positive association. Option (b) is correct.

2018-Q25.shortcut: Statements 1 and 2 are the standard verbal definitions of positive and negative association. Statement 3 misdefines independence as a 'linear relationship' - independence means NO relationship at all. So 1 and 2 only.
tips: Independence of attributes means (AB) = (A)(B)/N, i.e. the observed joint frequency equals the product of the marginals. Nothing about linearity is involved - linearity belongs to correlation of variables, not association of attributes.
The examiner's favourite trap in this chapter is importing correlation language (linear, positive, negative) into attribute theory. Read every option for that swap.
Association compares (AB) with (A)(B)/N: greater means positive association, smaller means negative association, equal means independence. Three cases, one formula.
Whenever one statement in a set is a definition that has been subtly reworded, that is almost always the false one - here statement 3.
solution: Two attributes A and B are said to be INDEPENDENT when (AB) = (A)(B)/N, where N is the total frequency.
Statement 1: A and B are positively associated when the presence of A tends to be accompanied by the presence of B, i.e. (AB) > (A)(B)/N. This is the standard verbal definition. TRUE.
Statement 2: A and B are negatively associated (disassociated) when the presence of one tends to exclude the other, i.e. (AB) < (A)(B)/N. TRUE.

Statement 3: independence is defined by the frequency identity above, not by any 'linear relationship'. Linearity is a concept of correlation between quantitative variables, not of association between attributes. FALSE.
Only statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option (b) is right.

2018-Q26.shortcut: Fix x and look at the y-part: f is proportional to e^(-y(1+x)), which is an Exponential with RATE (1+x). Its mean is the reciprocal, so E(Y|X=x) = 1/(1+x).
tips: The regression of Y on X IS the conditional mean E(Y|X=x). Whenever the joint density factorises as g(x) e^(-y h(x)), the conditional law of Y is Exponential(h(x)) and the answer is 1/h(x) - one line, no integration.
Any multiplicative function of x alone (here x^2/3) is absorbed into the normalising constant of the conditional density and cannot appear in E(Y|X). That rules out options (b) and (d) at a glance.
Option (c) y = 1 + x inverts the relationship: it is the RATE, not the mean. Reciprocal errors are the standard trap in exponential conditionals.

Note that the printed joint density is not normalisable over the stated range (the x-integral of x^2/(1+x) diverges), but the conditional distribution of Y given X - and hence the answer - is unaffected.
solution: The joint density is f(x,y) = (1/3) x^2 e^(-y(1+x)) for x >= 0, y >= 0.
For a fixed value X = x, the conditional density of Y is f(y|x) = f(x,y)/f_X(x), which is proportional to e^(-y(1+x)) for y >= 0.
Normalising, f(y|x) = (1 + x) e^(-y(1+x)), which is the Exponential density with rate parameter (1 + x).
The mean of an Exponential distribution with rate lambda is 1/lambda, so E(Y | X = x) = 1/(1 + x).
The regression of Y on X is the curve y = E(Y|X = x) = 1/(1 + x).
Hence option (a) is correct.

2018-Q27.shortcut: All three are standard properties of the bivariate normal: zero correlation gives independence, every linear combination is normal, and both regression lines are linear with constant (homoscedastic) conditional variance. Answer: all three.
tips: 'rho = 0 implies independence' is TRUE for the bivariate normal and FALSE in general - the examiner exploits this asymmetry constantly. Check whether normality is stated.
The conditional variance of Y given X is sigma_2^2(1 - rho^2), which does not depend on x. That constancy is exactly what homoscedasticity means.
The conditional mean is E(Y|X=x) = mu_2 + rho (sigma_2/sigma_1)(x - mu_1) - linear in x, which gives the linear regression property.
In a 1/2/3 item where every statement is a bookwork property of the same distribution, (d) 'all of them' is very often the key - but confirm the one you are least sure of, here statement 3.
solution: Statement 1: for the bivariate normal, the joint density factorises into the product of the two marginal normal densities precisely when rho = 0. So independence holds if and only if rho = 0. TRUE. (Note this equivalence is special to the normal; in general rho = 0 does not imply independence.)
Statement 2: if (X,Y) is bivariate normal then aX + bY is univariate normal for all constants a, b - this is a defining property of the multivariate normal family. TRUE.
Statement 3: the conditional distribution of Y given X = x is N(mu_2 + rho (sigma_2/sigma_1)(x - mu_1), sigma_2^2(1 - rho^2)).

The conditional mean is linear in x, so the regression of Y on X is linear; the conditional variance sigma_2^2(1 - rho^2) is free of x, so the regression is homoscedastic. By symmetry the same holds for X on Y. TRUE.
All three statements are correct, so option (d) is right.

2018-Q28.shortcut: Correlation is invariant under a change of origin. Adding 3 to every Maths mark shifts the origin only, so r is unchanged at 0.65.
tips: r is invariant under any change of origin and under a change of scale by a POSITIVE constant; multiplying by a negative constant flips only the sign, never the magnitude.
The sample size 60 is deliberately irrelevant here - the examiner adds it purely as a distraction.
Formally, Cov(X + c, Y) = Cov(X, Y) and Var(X + c) = Var(X), so every ingredient of r is unchanged.
Option (d) 'almost 1' punishes the belief that a systematic adjustment somehow strengthens the relationship - the scatter pattern is simply translated.
solution: Let X be Maths marks and Y be Statistics marks, with r(X,Y) = 0.65.
The revised Maths marks are X' = X + 3, a pure change of origin.
Covariance is unaffected by a shift: Cov(X + 3, Y) = Cov(X, Y).
Variance is also unaffected: Var(X + 3) = Var(X), so sd(X') = sd(X).
Therefore r(X', Y) = Cov(X',Y)/(sd(X') sd(Y)) = Cov(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y)) = r(X,Y) = 0.65.
Hence option (b) is correct.

2018-Q29.shortcut: Put r12 = r13 = r23 = rho in R^2 = (r12^2 + r13^2 - 2 r12 r13 r23)/(1 - r23^2). Numerator = 2rho^2 - 2rho^3 = 2rho^2(1-rho); denominator = (1-rho)(1+rho). Cancel (1-rho) to get 2rho^2/(1+rho).
tips: Memorise R^2_(1.23) = (r12^2 + r13^2 - 2 r12 r13 r23)/(1 - r23^2). Every multiple-correlation numerical in this paper reduces to it.
The cancellation of (1 - rho) is the whole trick; factor 1 - rho^2 as (1-rho)(1+rho) before simplifying rather than after.
Check the limits: rho = 0 must give R^2 = 0 (option (b) gives 0, correct) and rho = 1 must give R^2 = 1 (option (b) gives 2/2 = 1, correct). Option (c) fails the rho = 1 test, giving 1/2.
R^2 is a squared quantity, so a bare rho as in option (a) cannot be right on dimensional grounds.
solution: The square of the multiple correlation of X1 on X2, X3 is R^2_(1.23) = (r12^2 + r13^2 - 2 r12 r13 r23)/(1 - r23^2).
All three zero-order correlations equal rho, so r12 = r13 = r23 = rho.
Numerator: rho^2 + rho^2 - 2 rho . rho . rho = 2rho^2 - 2rho^3 = 2rho^2 (1 - rho).
Denominator: 1 - rho^2 = (1 - rho)(1 + rho).
Cancelling the common factor (1 - rho) gives R^2_(1.23) = 2rho^2/(1 + rho).
Hence option (b) is correct.

2018-Q30.shortcut: Under rho = 0 the density of r is proportional to (1 - r^2)^((N-4)/2). Multiplying by (1-r^2)^(-1) lowers the exponent by one, so the expectation is a ratio of Beta functions that collapses to (N-3)/(N-4).
tips: Null density to memorise: f(r) = (1 - r^2)^((N-4)/2) / B(1/2, (N-2)/2) on (-1, 1). Almost every 'distribution of r when rho = 0' item is solved by shifting its exponent.
The standard integral is: integral over (-1,1) of (1 - r^2)^(a-1) dr = B(1/2, a). Recognising the integrand as a Beta kernel converts the whole problem into Gamma-function algebra.
Use Gamma(z+1) = z Gamma(z) and Gamma(z + 3/2) = (z + 1/2) Gamma(z + 1/2) - after those two substitutions everything cancels except (N-3)/(N-4).
Sanity check with large N: the answer must tend to 1 because r tends to 0 and (1-r^2)^(-1) tends to 1. Only options (a) and (d) do that, and (d) ignores N entirely.
solution: When the population correlation is zero, the density of the sample correlation coefficient based on N observations is f(r) = (1 - r^2)^((N-4)/2) / B(1/2, (N-2)/2), for -1 < r < 1.
Hence E[(1 - r^2)^(-1)] = [1/B(1/2, (N-2)/2)] times the integral over (-1,1) of (1 - r^2)^((N-6)/2) dr.
Using the standard result integral over (-1,1) of (1 - r^2)^(a-1) dr = B(1/2, a), with a - 1 = (N-6)/2 so that a = (N-4)/2, the integral equals B(1/2, (N-4)/2).
Writing B(1/2, a) = Gamma(1/2)Gamma(a)/Gamma(a + 1/2) and putting a1 = (N-4)/2, a2 = a1 + 1, the ratio becomes [Gamma(a1) Gamma(a1 + 3/2)] / [Gamma(a1 + 1/2) Gamma(a1 + 1)].
Using Gamma(a1 + 1) = a1 Gamma(a1) and Gamma(a1 + 3/2) = (a1 + 1/2) Gamma(a1 + 1/2), this equals (a1 + 1/2)/a1 = [(N-3)/2]/[(N-4)/2] = (N-3)/(N-4), option (a).

2018-Q31.shortcut: An exact linear relation makes the two residuals proportional. From a x1 + b x2 + c x3 = 0 we get x1 = -(b/a)x2 - (c/a)x3, so after removing x3 the residual of x1 is a NEGATIVE multiple of that of x2 (for a, b of the same sign), giving r12.3 = -1.
tips: Exact linear dependence always forces a partial correlation of magnitude 1 - so the real question is only the sign, and options (a) and (d) can be struck out at once.
Sign rule: r12.3 = -sign(b/a). With the usual textbook convention that a, b, c are positive constants (as in the classic x1 + x2 + x3 = 0), the value is -1.
The formula r12.3 = (r12 - r13 r23)/sqrt((1 - r13^2)(1 - r23^2)) also gives +-1 here, but the residual argument reaches the sign far faster.
Partial correlation removes the linear effect of x3 from BOTH variables; what remains is the pure x1-x2 link, which is deterministic here.
solution: The relation a x1 + b x2 + c x3 = 0 holds identically, so the three variables are exactly linearly dependent.
Solve for x1: x1 = -(b/a) x2 - (c/a) x3.
Regress each of x1 and x2 on x3 and take residuals. Because the relation above is exact, the residual of x1 after removing x3 equals -(b/a) times the residual of x2 after removing x3.
A residual pair related by an exact multiplicative constant has correlation +1 if the constant is positive and -1 if it is negative.
Here the constant is -(b/a), which is negative when a and b have the same sign - the standard convention in this classical result (e.g. the case x1 + x2 + x3 = 0).
Hence r12.3 = -1, option (c). (If a and b had opposite signs the value would be +1; the magnitude is always 1.)

2018-Q32.shortcut: U and V share X1 and X2. Cov(U,V) = Var(X1) + Var(X2) = 2 sigma^2, while Var(U) = Var(V) = 3 sigma^2. So r = 2 sigma^2/(3 sigma^2) = 2/3.
tips: For sums of uncorrelated variables with a common variance, the correlation is simply (number of SHARED terms)/sqrt(count in U x count in V). Here 2/sqrt(3 x 3) = 2/3.
Uncorrelated cross terms vanish, so the covariance counts only the overlap - never expand all nine products.
sigma^2 cancels completely, which is why the answer is a pure number; if your working leaves a sigma you have slipped.
Extreme checks: no shared terms would give 0 and complete overlap would give 1, so a two-out-of-three overlap must land strictly between - eliminating (a) and (b).
solution: X1, X2, X3, X4 are uncorrelated, each with variance sigma^2, so all cross-covariances are 0.
Var(U) = Var(X1 + X2 + X3) = 3 sigma^2, and similarly Var(V) = Var(X1 + X2 + X4) = 3 sigma^2.
Cov(U, V) = Cov(X1 + X2 + X3, X1 + X2 + X4). Every cross term between distinct variables is 0, so only the shared variables contribute.
Cov(U, V) = Var(X1) + Var(X2) = sigma^2 + sigma^2 = 2 sigma^2.
Therefore r(U, V) = 2 sigma^2 / sqrt(3 sigma^2 . 3 sigma^2) = 2 sigma^2/(3 sigma^2) = 2/3.
Hence option (d) is correct.

2018-Q33.shortcut: For U[-3,3], mean = 0 and variance = (6)^2/12 = 3. By the CLT, sqrt(n) (Xbar - mu) converges to N(0, sigma^2) = N(0, 3). No division by sigma appears, so the variance stays 3.
tips: Variance of U[a,b] is (b-a)^2/12. Here (3 - (-3))^2/12 = 36/12 = 3 - compute this before anything else.
Distinguish the two CLT forms: sqrt(n) Xbar / sigma tends to N(0,1) whereas sqrt(n) Xbar tends to N(0, sigma^2). The stem has no sigma in the denominator, so option (b) not (a).
The limit is NORMAL, never uniform - the CLT destroys the parent shape. Options (c) and (d) are eliminated on principle without any arithmetic.
The mean of U[-a,a] is 0 by symmetry, which is why the limiting mean is 0 and no centring constant is needed.
solution: For the Uniform distribution on [-3, 3], the mean is mu = (-3 + 3)/2 = 0 and the variance is sigma^2 = (3 - (-3))^2/12 = 36/12 = 3.
The Central Limit Theorem states that sqrt(n)(Xbar - mu)/sigma converges in distribution to N(0, 1) as n grows.
Since mu = 0, this reads sqrt(n) Xbar / sigma tends to N(0,1).
Multiplying by the constant sigma, sqrt(n) Xbar converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2) = N(0, 3).
Hence the large-sample distribution is N(0, 3), option (b).

tips: sqrt(900) = 30 is the only arithmetic that matters; 2.1/30 = 0.07 makes the z-score a clean -1.43, which is exactly the value the examiner supplies.
The supplied figure P(0 < Z < 1.43) = 0.4236 is a CENTRAL area, not a tail. The left tail is 0.5 - 0.4236 = 0.0764 - subtracting from 0.5, never from 1.
Option (b) 0.6408 = 0.5 + 0.1408 and option (d) 0.7046 are built from misreading the table; option (c) 0.6074 is 0.5 + 0.1074. All assume the wrong tail.
Sanity check: the population mean 0.1 is positive and the sample is large, so a negative sample mean should be UNLIKELY - the answer must be well below 0.5, which only (a) is.
solution: The population has mean mu = 0.1 and standard deviation sigma = 2.1; the sample size is n = 900.
The standard error of the sample mean is sigma/sqrt(n) = 2.1/30 = 0.07.
We need P(Xbar < 0). Standardising: z = (0 - 0.1)/0.07 = -1.4286, which rounds to -1.43.
P(Xbar < 0) = P(Z < -1.43) = P(Z > 1.43) by symmetry.
Using the supplied value P(0 < Z < 1.43) = 0.4236, we get P(Z > 1.43) = 0.5 - 0.4236 = 0.0764.
Hence option (a) is correct.

2018-Q35.shortcut: Build t = Z/sqrt(chi^2_3/3). Here Z = (X1+X2)/sqrt(2) and chi^2_3 = X3^2+X4^2+X5^2, so t = sqrt(3)(X1+X2)/(sqrt(2) sqrt(sum)). Hence C = sqrt(3)/sqrt(2) = sqrt(3/2).
tips: The t-statistic template is ALWAYS standard normal divided by sqrt(chi-square/its own d.f.). Identify the two pieces and their d.f. before touching the algebra.
X1 + X2 has variance 2, so it must be divided by sqrt(2) to become standard normal. Forgetting this gives sqrt(3) and no matching option.
The d.f. is 3 (three squared normals), so the divisor inside the square root is 3 - that is where the sqrt(3) in the numerator comes from.
sqrt(3/2) = sqrt(6)/2 = 1.2247 while sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866; option (a) is the trap for candidates who take the square root of 3 but not of 2.
solution: X1, ..., X5 are independent N(0,1).
X3^2 + X4^2 + X5^2 ~ chi-square with 3 degrees of freedom, and it is independent of X1 + X2.
By definition, t = Z / sqrt(chi-square_3 / 3) follows Student's t with 3 d.f.
Substituting: t = [(X1+X2)/sqrt(2)] / sqrt((X3^2+X4^2+X5^2)/3) = sqrt(3)(X1+X2) / [sqrt(2) sqrt(X3^2+X4^2+X5^2)].
Comparing with C(X1+X2)/(X3^2+X4^2+X5^2)^(1/2) gives C = sqrt(3)/sqrt(2) = sqrt(3/2), option (b).

2018-Q36.shortcut: E(X) = n/(n-2) for X ~ F(m,n). Since 1/X ~ F(n,m), swapping the roles gives E(1/X) = m/(m-2). The product is mn/((m-2)(n-2)).
tips: The reciprocal property 1/F(m,n) ~ F(n,m) is the key. Once you have it, E(1/X) needs no integration - just swap m and n in the mean formula.
Remember the mean of F(m,n) involves only the DENOMINATOR d.f.: E = n/(n-2), n > 2. Candidates who use m/(m-2) for E(X) land on option (b), the mirror-image trap.
The conditions m > 2 and n > 2 in the stem exist precisely so that both expectations are finite - they are a hint about which formula to use.
By Jensen's inequality E(X)E(1/X) >= 1 always. Option (c) gives mn/((m-2)(n-2)) > 1 for all admissible m, n, which is the only option guaranteed to satisfy this.
solution: For X ~ F(m, n) with n > 2, the mean is E(X) = n/(n - 2).
A standard property of the F distribution is that 1/X ~ F(n, m), i.e. the degrees of freedom interchange.
Applying the mean formula to 1/X ~ F(n, m), whose denominator d.f. is now m, gives E(1/X) = m/(m - 2), valid since m > 2.
Hence option (c) is correct.

2018-Q37.shortcut: Both the chi-square goodness-of-fit test and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compare an observed distribution with a completely specified theoretical one. K-S is the distribution-free analogue.
tips: Sort the non-parametric tests by what they compare: goodness of fit to a specified distribution = chi-square and K-S (one sample); two independent samples = Mann-Whitney and median test; paired/matched data = Wilcoxon signed-rank and sign test; randomness = run test.
Chi-square needs GROUPED data with adequate expected frequencies; K-S works directly on the ungrouped empirical CDF and is therefore preferred for small samples and continuous data.
K-S uses the maximum absolute deviation D = sup |F_n(x) - F_0(x)| - remember it as a 'largest vertical gap between two CDFs' test.
Mann-Whitney (option a) and Wilcoxon (option c) are location-comparison tests, and the median test (option d) compares medians - none of them tests fit to a specified distribution.
solution: The chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares observed frequencies with the frequencies expected under a fully specified theoretical distribution.
Among the listed non-parametric procedures, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov one-sample test performs the same task: it compares the empirical distribution function F_n(x) with a hypothesised F_0(x).
The K-S statistic is D = sup over x of |F_n(x) - F_0(x)|, the largest vertical distance between the two curves, and a large D leads to rejection of the hypothesised distribution.
The Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests compare locations of samples, and the median test compares medians; none of them tests agreement with a specified distribution.
Hence the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the analogue of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test, option (b).

2018-Q38.shortcut: Statement 1 reverses the relationship - the SQUARE of a standard normal is chi-square(1), not the other way round - so it is false. Statements 2 and 3 are standard results, giving 2 and 3 only.
tips: Correct direction: Z ~ N(0,1) implies Z^2 ~ chi-square(1). The normal is not a special case of the chi-square; the chi-square family is built FROM normals.
Moment rule for t with n d.f.: E(t^k) exists only for k < n. The t with 1 d.f. is the Cauchy, which has no mean at all - a good anchor for remembering the rule.
t_n^2 ~ F(1, n) is worth memorising alongside F(m,n) = 1/F(n,m) and chi-square(n)/n as n grows tending to 1. These three identities cover most sampling-distribution items.
Where one statement asserts a containment between distribution families, check the DIRECTION of the containment - reversal is the single most common falsification device.
solution: Statement 1: the chi-square with 1 degree of freedom is the distribution of Z^2 where Z ~ N(0,1). The normal itself is not a chi-square; the chi-square is non-negative and skewed while the normal is symmetric on the whole line. FALSE.
Statement 2: for Student's t with n degrees of freedom, the tail behaves like |t|^(-(n+1)), so E(|t|^k) is finite exactly when k < n. Hence all moments of order less than n exist. TRUE.

Statement 3: write t = Z/sqrt(V/n) with Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ chi-square(n) independent. Then t^2 = Z^2/(V/n) = (Z^2/1)/(V/n), a ratio of independent chi-squares divided by their degrees of freedom, which is F(1, n). TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct, so option (c) is right.

2018-Q39.shortcut: min(X1,X2) = [(X1+X2) - |X1-X2|]/2. The first term has mean 0 and X1 - X2 ~ N(0, 2 sigma^2), so E|X1-X2| = sigma sqrt(2) . sqrt(2/pi) = 2 sigma/sqrt(pi). Hence E[X_(1)] = -sigma/sqrt(pi).
tips: Identity worth memorising: min(a,b) = (a + b - |a - b|)/2 and max(a,b) = (a + b + |a - b|)/2. It converts order-statistic expectations into a mean-absolute-deviation computation.
For W ~ N(0, tau^2), E|W| = tau sqrt(2/pi). Here tau = sigma sqrt(2), so E|X1 - X2| = 2 sigma/sqrt(pi).
Sign check first: the minimum of two symmetric mean-zero variables must have a NEGATIVE expectation, which immediately eliminates options (a) and (b).
For a sample of size 2 from any symmetric distribution, E[X_(1)] = -E[X_(2)]; the two order statistics are mirror images about the mean.
solution: Let X1, X2 be independent N(0, sigma^2) and let X_(1) = min(X1, X2).
Use the identity min(X1, X2) = [(X1 + X2) - |X1 - X2|]/2.
E(X1 + X2) = 0 since both means are 0.
X1 - X2 ~ N(0, 2 sigma^2), so with tau = sigma sqrt(2) and the half-normal mean formula E|W| = tau sqrt(2/pi), we get E|X1 - X2| = sigma sqrt(2) . sqrt(2/pi) = 2 sigma/sqrt(pi).
Therefore E[X_(1)] = [0 - 2 sigma/sqrt(pi)]/2 = -sigma/sqrt(pi).
Hence option (c) is correct.

2018-Q40.shortcut: For a U(0,1) sample the range R ~ Beta(n-1, 2), whose density is n(n-1) r^(n-2)(1-r) on (0,1). Recognise the Beta and read the answer off.
tips: General range density: g(r) = n(n-1) times the integral over x of f(x) f(x+r) [F(x+r) - F(x)]^(n-2) dx. For U(0,1) the bracket is just r and the integral contributes the factor (1 - r).
Shape check: R ~ Beta(n-1, 2) means the exponents must be (n-1)-1 = n-2 on r and 2-1 = 1 on (1-r). Only option (a) has that pairing; option (b) has them swapped.
Normalisation test: the integral of n(n-1) r^(n-2)(1-r) over (0,1) is n(n-1) [1/(n-1) - 1/n] = 1. Option (b) also integrates to 1, so use the shape argument, not normalisation, to separate them.
Options (c) and (d) are densities of the MAXIMUM and of a related order statistic, not of the range - a classic substitution trap.
solution: The X_i are i.i.d. Uniform(0,1), so f(x) = 1 on (0,1) and F(x) = x on (0,1).
The joint density of the smallest and largest order statistics is h(u, v) = n(n-1) f(u) f(v) [F(v) - F(u)]^(n-2) = n(n-1)(v - u)^(n-2) for 0 < u < v < 1.
Put R = V - U and integrate out U. For a fixed r in (0,1), U can range over (0, 1 - r).
g(r) = integral from 0 to 1-r of n(n-1) r^(n-2) du = n(n-1) r^(n-2) (1 - r), for 0 < r < 1.
This is the Beta(n-1, 2) density, and it integrates to n(n-1)[1/(n-1) - 1/n] = 1, confirming correctness.
Hence option (a) is correct.
